chapter.title: Design a News Feed System
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Design a scalable news feed system in which users can publish posts and view friends' posts in reverse chronological order, while supporting media content, fast feed retrieval, efficient fanout, caching, authentication, rate limiting, and large-scale operation.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 11 designs a news feed system similar to Facebook News Feed, Instagram feed, or Twitter timeline. The simplified requirements support both web and mobile clients, allow users to publish posts and view friends' posts, sort feeds in reverse chronological order, allow up to 5,000 friends per user, serve 10 million daily active users, and support image/video media. The architecture is organized around two major flows: feed publishing and news feed retrieval. Publishing persists a post in database/cache, fans the post out to friends, and may trigger notifications. Retrieval reads precomputed feed IDs from cache and hydrates them with user and post objects. The deep dive compares fanout on write versus fanout on read and selects a hybrid model: push for most users, pull for celebrities or high-fanout users. The fanout pipeline uses a graph database for friend IDs, user cache for friend metadata/settings, a message queue, fanout workers, and a news feed cache that stores IDs rather than full objects. Media is served through a CDN, and the cache tier is divided into news feed, content, social graph, action, and counter layers. The wrap-up highlights database scaling, stateless web servers, aggressive caching, multi-data-center support, message-queue decoupling, and monitoring.
chapter_summary.selected_fanout_strategy: Hybrid: fanout-on-write/push for most users, fanout-on-read/pull for celebrities or users with many friends/followers.

core_features: A user can publish a post.
A user can see friends' posts on the news feed page.

news_feed_definition.source_summary: A constantly updating list of stories containing items such as status updates, photos, videos, links, app activity, and likes from people, pages, and groups a user follows.

feed_publishing.definition: When a user publishes a post, the post is written to cache and database, and the post is populated to friends' news feeds.

news_feed_building.definition: Build the feed by aggregating friends' posts in reverse chronological order.

parameters.auth_token: Used to authenticate the API request.
Used to authenticate the API request.

Persists the post in database and cache.

Informs friends that new content is available and sends push notifications.
Route the request to the news feed service.
Fetches news feed data from cache.
Stores feed IDs needed to render the feed.

web_server_deep_dive.authentication_rule: Only users signed in with a valid auth_token may make posts.
web_server_deep_dive.rate_limiting_rule: Limit how many posts a user can make during a time period to prevent spam and abusive content.

fanout.definition: The process of delivering a post to all friends.

fanout_on_write.mechanism: Pre-compute the news feed at write time by immediately delivering a new post into friends' feed caches.
pros: News feed is generated in real time and can be pushed immediately.
Feed retrieval is fast because the feed is already precomputed.
cons: Users with many friends require expensive friend-list lookup and feed generation for many recipients.
The chapter calls this a hotkey problem.
Precomputing feeds for inactive or rarely active users wastes computing resources.

fanout_on_read.mechanism: Generate the news feed at read time by pulling recent posts when the user loads the home page.
pros: Does not waste compute precomputing feeds for inactive users.
No fanout hotkey problem because data is not pushed to all friends.
cons: Feed retrieval is slower because the feed was not precomputed.

selected_hybrid.majority_of_users: Use push/fanout-on-write because fast retrieval is important.
selected_hybrid.celebrities_or_high_degree_users: Use pull/fanout-on-read so followers fetch content on demand rather than forcing a massive write fanout.
selected_hybrid.hotkey_mitigation: Consistent hashing can distribute requests/data more evenly and help mitigate hotkey pressure.

fanout_service_workflow.action: Fetch friend IDs from the graph database.
fanout_service_workflow.reason: Graph databases are suitable for friend relationships and friend recommendations.

fanout_service_workflow.action: Fetch friends' information from user cache and filter according to user settings.
examples: Muted friend's posts should not appear.
Selective sharing may hide a post from some friends.

fanout_service_workflow.action: Send the friends list and new post ID to the message queue.
Fanout workers pull from the message queue and write feed data to the news feed cache.
Store <post_id, user_id> in the news feed cache.

feed_cache_design.why_ids_only: Storing complete user and post objects in feed cache would consume too much memory.
feed_cache_design.size_policy: Use a configurable maximum because users are unlikely to scroll through thousands of posts and are usually interested in recent content.
feed_cache_design.effect: The chapter expects a low cache-miss rate for this bounded recent-feed cache.

news_feed_retrieval_deep_dive.media_storage: Images, videos, and other media are stored in a CDN for fast retrieval.

steps.action: Load balancer distributes the request to web servers.
Web servers call the news feed service.
News feed service retrieves a list of post IDs from news feed cache.
News feed service fetches complete user and post objects from user cache and post cache to construct a fully hydrated feed.
Return the fully hydrated feed to the client as JSON for rendering.

cache_architecture.importance: The chapter states that cache is extremely important to a news feed system.

layers.specialization: Popular content is stored in hot cache.

layers.stores: User relationship data such as follower/following.
Information about likes, replies, and other user actions on posts.
Like, reply, follower, following, and other counters.

other_talking_points: Cache data as much as possible.
Use message queues to decouple components.
example_metrics: Latency while users refresh their news feed
wrap_up_scaling_topics.source_wording_note: The source prints 'Lose couple components with message queues'; this guide interprets the intended architectural point as decoupling components with message queues while preserving the source's meaning.

short_answer_questions.question: Describe the two core system flows.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Publishing persists a post and fans it out to friends' feed caches, while retrieval reads feed IDs and constructs the user's visible feed from cached user/post data.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare fanout on write and fanout on read.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Fanout on write precomputes recipient feeds when a post is created, producing fast reads but expensive writes and wasted work for inactive users. Fanout on read delays aggregation until the feed is requested, saving write-side work but making feed reads slower.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is a hybrid fanout model selected?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Fast feed retrieval is important for most users, so push is used by default. Extremely high-fanout users such as celebrities would overload a push model, so their followers pull those posts on demand.

short_answer_questions.question: Walk through the fanout service.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Fetch friend IDs from graph DB, fetch/filter friend information using user cache and settings, enqueue the friend list and post ID, let fanout workers consume the queue, and store <post_id,user_id> feed entries in news feed cache.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does news feed cache store IDs instead of complete objects?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Replicating full user/post objects into every recipient's feed cache would consume too much memory. The design stores lightweight IDs and hydrates the objects later from dedicated caches.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain detailed news feed retrieval.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The request reaches web servers through a load balancer, web servers call News Feed Service, the service reads post IDs from News Feed Cache, fetches full user and post objects from their caches, constructs the hydrated feed, and returns it as JSON.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the five-layer cache architecture.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: News Feed stores feed IDs; Content stores post data with popular content in hot cache; Social Graph stores relationship data; Action stores liked/replied/other action state; Counters stores numerical counts such as likes, replies, followers, and following.

short_answer_questions.question: What should you discuss if the interviewer asks how to scale the design further?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Database vertical/horizontal scaling, SQL versus NoSQL, replication/read replicas, consistency, sharding, stateless web servers, aggressive caching, multiple data centers, message-queue decoupling, and operational monitoring.

common_confusions.confusion: Fanout on write means the post is written only once.
common_confusions.correction: It means recipient news feeds are precomputed at write time, which can create substantial fanout work.

common_confusions.confusion: Fanout on read is always better because it avoids write amplification.
common_confusions.correction: It makes retrieval slower, so the chapter uses push for most users because fast feed reads are crucial.

common_confusions.confusion: The chapter uses push fanout for celebrities too.
common_confusions.correction: Celebrities/high-fanout users are handled with pull-on-read in the hybrid model.

common_confusions.confusion: Friendship alone determines whether a post appears.
common_confusions.correction: User settings such as mute and selective sharing can filter otherwise valid friend relationships.

common_confusions.confusion: News Feed Cache stores full post/user objects.
common_confusions.correction: It stores IDs to reduce memory usage; full objects are fetched later from user/post caches.

common_confusions.confusion: The feed cache must retain every historical post.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter uses a configurable limit because users mostly care about recent content.

common_confusions.confusion: Post images and videos are served from the same feed-ID cache.
common_confusions.correction: Media content is stored in a CDN for fast retrieval.

common_confusions.confusion: One generic cache is enough to describe the design.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter explicitly separates caching into News Feed, Content, Social Graph, Action, and Counters layers.

practice_problems.prompt: If every one of 10 million DAU had the maximum 5,000 friends, how many user-friend relationship references would that represent before accounting for symmetry/deduplication?
practice_problems.note: Derived study calculation from chapter requirements; the chapter does not provide this number.

practice_problems.prompt: A user with 100 friends publishes often and most friends read feeds frequently. Which default fanout model fits the chapter's strategy?
practice_problems.solution: Fanout on write/push because fast reads are prioritized and fanout size is manageable.

practice_problems.prompt: A celebrity with massive followers publishes once per hour. Which model should be applied to that celebrity's content?
practice_problems.solution: Fanout on read/pull for that high-fanout user's content.

practice_problems.prompt: Why not store 10,000 fully hydrated feed objects per user in the News Feed Cache?
practice_problems.solution: The chapter warns that full user/post objects would consume large amounts of memory, and users rarely scroll through thousands of posts. Store bounded IDs and hydrate on read instead.

practice_problems.prompt: Choose the cache layer for each datum: post body, follower relationship, has-liked state, like count.
practice_problems.solution: Post body -> Content; follower relationship -> Social Graph; has-liked -> Action; like count -> Counters.

practice_problems.prompt: Place these in order: return JSON, fetch post IDs, fetch user/post objects, request feed.
practice_problems.solution: Request feed -> fetch post IDs -> fetch user/post objects -> return JSON.

must_memorize: Requirements: web + mobile, publish/read feeds, reverse chronological, max 5,000 friends, 10M DAU, media support.
Two flows: feed publishing and news feed retrieval.
POST /v1/me/feed publishes; GET /v1/me/feed retrieves.
Publishing: user -> LB -> web -> Post Service/Fanout Service/Notification Service.
Retrieval: user -> LB -> web -> News Feed Service -> News Feed Cache.
Web servers enforce authentication and rate limiting.
Fanout = delivering a post to friends/followers.
Fanout on write = push/precompute; fast reads but hotkey and wasted inactive-user compute.
Fanout on read = pull/on-demand; avoids push hotkey but slower reads.
Hybrid: push for most users, pull celebrity/high-fanout content.
Consistent hashing can help distribute hotkey load.
Fanout pipeline: graph DB -> user cache/filter -> queue -> fanout workers -> feed cache.
Graph DB stores/manages friendship relationships.
Mute/selective sharing can filter posts from a feed.
News feed cache stores <post_id,user_id>, not full objects.
Bound feed-cache depth because users care mostly about recent content.
Media is served from CDN.
Retrieval reads feed IDs then hydrates with user/post caches.
Final feed is returned as JSON.
Five cache layers: News Feed, Content, Social Graph, Action, Counters.
Wrap-up: database scale, stateless web tier, aggressive caching, multi-DC, message queues, monitoring.
chapter_eleven_final_review.memory_chain: PUBLISH -> POST SERVICE -> FANOUT -> GRAPH FRIENDS -> USER SETTINGS -> QUEUE -> FANOUT WORKERS -> FEED ID CACHE || READ -> FEED IDS -> USER/POST CACHE HYDRATION -> JSON + CDN MEDIA || HYBRID PUSH/PULL + 5-LAYER CACHE
chapter_eleven_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: A scalable news feed system precomputes lightweight feed entries for most users, uses pull-on-read for high-fanout authors, hydrates cached feed IDs into full posts at read time, and relies heavily on caches, queues, graph relationships, and stateless horizontally scalable services.
